First of all, don't see Orwell as a game, but as an experience. Gameplay-wise, it isn't the most advanced thing out there, it's just a click-and-drag with some choices.
What's interesting with Orwell, is the story, the choices, and the questions it brings to your mind. It will make you reflect on mass spying, sacrificing privacy for safety, and other topics relatable as of today.

I'll end this review by saying that if you loved "1984", well this game's for you.

Orwell is this game about the simple pleasure of peeking into other people's lives and having absolute power over their privacies. As a government agent with almost total access to suspect's private information, your job is to find out the truth behind a terrorist attack. Things, of course, as not as simple as they seem, and they keep getting weirder and weirder until you reach the end of the line and realize where your choices have led you, and those you interacted with without their knowledge. 

Orwell is a unique, twisted and smart game, and it works. I finished one playthrough in about four hours and might do more to uncover the outcome of those choices I didn't make. If you enjoy thrilling stories, enthralling mysteries, interface-based gameplay and that amazing feeling of looking at information you should most likely not be allowed to look at, try this game out.

I must say I had high expectations for this game considering the current climate of data-collection and mass surveillance. Little did I know I was in for a boring ride! 

At first, you're guided with what info can be considered relevant or not; if you make mistakes along the way your "supervior" reminds you of the mission at hand. So that's definitely a good start, especially for chapter 1. 
But then, I expected players would be gradually given more leeway as to what info to select and upload on Orwell servers. And so as the story unfolded the whole thing felt too scripted, too one-way track, and it lost its original twist. The team tries to make up for it by adding a new rule near the end; that came too late for me. 

Also, let's talk about the ending: if you're like me and you'd already figured what was really going on 2 chapters ago, it was just dragging on for too long, with all the explanations and all. Sometimes, it's best to keep it short - better, a little cryptic -, that way it leaves room for players to engage and connect the dots.
The soundtrack was nice for most of the part except when it got all ominous - a way to tell you you've come across some serious, plot-twist info: would've been nice to try and figure it out on my own.

Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game,

Long over due review for this game. Maybe a few spoilers in it so read if you want. Orwell is a strange game. More like a simulation if you would. It places you as an investigator of a top secret internet detective group. Your primary means of investigation is literally spying on the general populace you are sworn to protect. It's also incredibly immersive with characters that have real life reactions to your actions and events that seem directly inspired by real life. You kind of forget you are playing again. Yes, you know what that spying on these people's personal lives is wrong, you know that taking their online jokes out of context is wrong, but you also know that if you don't do your job people are going to die and it's going to be your fault for not having properly acted on the bits of truth you have. 

It's very crazy. Being forced to piece together elaborate truths based merely shreds of evidence scattered across the web, not knowing if the information you are gathering will be relevant or even lead you to your next clue, trying to minimize the damage of your actions on those you think are innocent while being fully aware you might have to drag them through the mud to get the info you need. They'll live, you know they will which almost justifies the mud you throw at them. Yet the people who're lives are being targeted. Those who are going to be hit the most by the extremists you hunt, unless you're willing to get your hands dirty, they won't live. 

I just finished my first real case to locate the next target of a domestic terrorist and shit I've never been so stressed in a game before. I had to threaten an innocent girl with charges of torture because she was being non-cooperative. It's a trumped charge, won't stick in 100 years and I know it was wrong, but it got her to talk. Got that last piece of evidence we needed to locate the bomb from her and with that my official report was submitted. Most games give you a reply immediately when you do things like this. Not Orwell. It makes you wait. it makes you stew in your methods, in the possibility you might be wrong. After several minutes I get word that the evacuation order was given and that the bomb squad is moving in to investigate. I unknowingly cross my fingers. I have to be right on this. If they find no device that means we were wrong about the location and more people will die. I have to be right. I did too many wrong things to fail. Seconds go by, minutes go by, feels longer. Finally, a report comes in. They found the bomb and disabled it. I sigh in relief as my fingers uncross and my body relaxes. We did it. We saved those people's lives. The girl might be in trouble for a bit, but her cooperation in saving those people's lives will be noted. Charges against her might be dropped. At the worse, probation for her unknowing association with a terrorist group, but she'll live. Everyone will today. 

And that's how my first case in Orwell the game went. Honestly, if you like immersive text based games, buy this. You won't regret it.

Good game - very intense, with an aquired taste in art/aesthetic that I personally enjoyed. It was quite philosophical. Also, unlike many of it's competing "episodic" games (looking at you Telltale), the choices you make genuinely affect the gameplay, as well as the endings (and yes, I did finish the job... like my playthrough of LiS, why wouldn't I continue the very thing I had done the entire game?). The gameplay is detailed and intelligent.

My biggest issue is, as with many episodic games, the short timespan. The game is very short - and this also includes periods of time where you can't do anything, such as during the phone call and text sections. Also, there isn't too much of a progression system - for example, one of the better mechanics called "Insider" is only given to you near the climax of the game's story, and it is only used for about a tenth of the game's span. 

All in all, I do thoroughly recommend the game, especially if you want an intense yet oddly chilled experience (think of it as like a UAV flying simulator, except more personal) as well as ethical thinking as a genuinely thought provoking insight to the current age of omnipresent technology. However, if you want something that you can keep playing (for example, endgame content, replay value etc), then it probably isn't for you.

Excellent little game demonstrating the risks involved in mass surveillance, automated and manual data processing and excessive government oversight without similar levels of accountability. While there are certainly benefits to such things, one has to also consider the costs - and this game does a great job of showing the potential costs vs benefits if you give it a bit of thought.

In terms of gameplay, I found it to be extremely immersive the first time through. There were, however, a few small problems (imo) with the design in that it can occasionally be easy to dead-end yourself if you overlook, or consider irrelevant, the particular piece of information that triggers the "next part" of the game. Then you're in a situation where you're just randomly adding bits of seemingly irrelevant information "until and/or in the hope of something happening". 

Since there can often be very little to indicate which bit of information moves the story along, and which bits are completely unrelated and will get you yelled at for spamming the system, it can be a touch annoying. It also gives some inkling of the extent to which "big data" can be monitoring your life and drawing potentially misleading conclusions about it. So, that's extra scary, I guess?

Unfortunately, the same things that make the game so immersive on the first playthrough (i.e. the semi-occasionally-real-time nature of phone-calls and stuff) also feels to be a detriment on later play throughs. For a conversation where you know exactly what's happening in it, and where there's no "real-time" element, I found no way to speed it up and it got pretty annoying. To the point where I'd just click a button to start the conversation off, then go watch a movie or whatever. Thank goodness for the Steam browser, because if you alt-tab out, you lose your ingame cursor (or at least, I did), so at least I still had something to do during some of the super-long-boring bits.

Overall, though, it's still an excellent game which I think everybody should play - even if just so they know what today's governments are getting up to!

I recommend it, IF you are interested in an epistolic, video-driven story rather than a game. Your choices feel very limited, and you must do certain things in order for the story to proceed, at which point you get fed another document, and you have to highlight certain things. Ultimately, you only make about 2 or 3 choices that actually matter in the outcome of the game.

However.....I thought the story was quite compelling, and the characters felt realistic. The game also provides a unique way of telling a story, from the standpoint of a government snoop. So if you want something that's a semi-interactive movie-novel, this is a good game for you. If you want something that's more a sandbox/choose your own adventure game, you'll be disappointed.
Buy it on sale.  ZERO REPLAYABILITY.

This is not a bad game, but I do think it's overrated. It falls short as a game and as a study of the surveillance state.

The gameplay mechanics are very simple -- you go to different links and and decide whether to upload them to Orwell or not. That's all there is to gameplay. Frustratingly, I ran into a few occasions where to advance the story I had to upload a link that was not obvious as to its value. Additionally, it's silly that you can't correct events later on, even before the information is acted upon -- if you send something over it's set in stone. And I'm not talking about the conflict choices -- those actually were good and created a good choice to have to make in deciding how the fate of certain people would go. 

Some of those negatives really betrayed the gamey-ness of the system. 

But worse was the whole conceit of the game really misses on being a meditation of surveillance gone awry. For one, the investigator is not a member of The Nation, which simply wouldn't happen in the real world, so it undercuts the influence of the government. The pressure that you as the investigator feels is thus negligble (unlike something like Papers, Please). The artificiality of the Orwell setup avoids the influence of government on media or bias of investigators that is very much an issue in the real world. 

Additionally, the game seems to suggest that the mere possibility of some people being investigated without having done wrong is evil. Except, that is how criminal investigations have gone since time immemorial. You start with some clues and investigate from there which will inevitably lead to some innocent people being scrutinized (even sometimes convicted). But that is the outcome of such a human operation and is not really a result of the surveillance state. And remember, we're investigating actual crimes where innocent people died. 

The game would have been much stronger if it showed intentional abuse by the system operators, influence by the government, or the ability to enact control of a population by knowing the way they think and act (think machine learning and how well it can predict certain behaviors/beliefs in people now). Or if the act in question was more dubious in nature, was maybe a false flag, or at least had some element of a frame up instead of an actual terrorist act committed by a true believer.

Another minor gripe is that you can't skip ahead on any chat or phone calls, which are interminably slow. While that might be realistic, it's also a bit boring.

The story also provides choices and branches in the same manner as a Telltale game, so if you like that facade you won't be bothered here. However, I did find it a bit unsatisfying that no matter the choices you made, the next episode would essentialy go the same way. And since everything is told in documents, calls, and chats, it's really lacking the dramatic power that a good Telltale game can have.

It wasn't a bad time but I definitely felt underwhelmed.

[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

In Orwell you take the role of an investigator working for the government to investigate a series of terror attacks.

Throughout the game you are presented with lots of pieces of information which you have to upload to a person's "file" to establish a character background to see if they're involved in the terror attacks. I found this gameplay mechanic to be thrilling. You tap phones, computers, emails - pretty much everything! At points you are presented with conflicting information between the suspects. This is were the story can change. In a sort of telltale like manner, your choices affect the outcome of the game and your consequences are final. 

I really enjoyed this game and found myself enagaged with each episode. I do wish it was longer, or maybe had some DLC cases added.

Basically, imagine a game where you spy on people and try to get to the bottom of crimes. That would be simple enough if it weren't for the sheer complexity and sleuthing and dilligence you need. It gets really intense when you have 2 different pieces of information that you're too under pressure to find out what is correct, so you just go on a whim.

Weither it was because of that, or because of the well timed sound effects (It was almost like a horror game at times, leaving me in a tiny bit of shock when certain events are uncovered or something suprising happens), I still consider this to be one of the better story telling games i've played, and i will buy the sequel as soon as i can to see how good it compares.
